video_title: We’re in a Debt Bubble — And Higher Rates, Inflation and AI Spending Are Adding Pressure
gist: Rocklinc CEO/CIO Jonathan Wellum tells Wealthion's Maggie Lake that persistent inflation, a ~$40T+ US debt load ($350T globally) and rising rates form a debt bubble that will force valuation compression, AI-capex write-offs, and a shift toward hard assets (gold, silver, copper, uranium) and short-duration bonds until rates peak.

insights.claim: The advisor's core thesis is that the economy is in a full-blown debt bubble that will produce overspending, overinvestment, corporate write-offs and broader financial damage, so investors should prioritize preservation of capital and purchasing power now.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Frame current markets as late-cycle/bubble-stage; tilt portfolios toward defensiveness and capital preservation rather than chasing risk assets.
insights.quote: There's going to be overspending and there's going to be overinvestment and that means there's going to be some write-offs and there's going to be some damage.

insights.claim: With roughly $42 trillion in US federal debt, even a below-market 3.75% average interest rate implies about $1.6 trillion in annual interest costs — roughly 26% of a projected $6 trillion revenue base next year, versus a historical 8-10% share, putting interest costs on track to exceed Social Security's 22% share of the federal budget within a year or two.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Rapidly rising interest costs as a share of the federal budget are a hard constraint on fiscal policy and a structural tailwind for higher-for-longer rates and eventual currency debasement/inflation.

insights.claim: The advisor cites roughly $350 trillion in total global debt as the backdrop for his concern that debt cannot simply be grown away, arguing this is a worldwide (not just US) problem also affecting Canada, France, the UK, Japan and China.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: A global, not just US-specific, debt overhang broadens the case for hard-asset and gold allocations across developed markets, not just US-dollar hedges.
insights.quote: we are very very concerned about 350 trillion in debt.

insights.claim: Trump's proposal of a $5,000 'dividend' to every American adult (an estimated $1.2+ trillion cost) is cited as evidence that the political mindset still assumes money can keep flowing freely, reinforcing the debt-bubble thesis rather than addressing it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Political incentives point toward continued deficit spending regardless of party, supporting a long-term inflation/debasement and gold thesis rather than a fiscal-discipline resolution.
insights.quote: he's going to give a $5,000 dividend to every, you know, American adult, which is like $1.2 plus trillion dollars.

insights.claim: If inflation stays somewhat elevated, price-earnings ratios should compress as rates rise and margins get squeezed, so investors should prioritize valuation discipline and favor businesses with pricing power and moats that can pass through costs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: A higher-inflation regime argues for rotating from high-multiple growth names toward moat-protected, pricing-power businesses and away from paying up for index-level valuations.
insights.quote: If inflation is going to remain a little higher that means price earnings ratio should actually come down.

insights.claim: Sticky inflation is partly attributed to fiscal overspending, money-supply growth, deglobalization, and now the Iran situation constraining refining/distillate capacity, which is pushing oil and diesel prices up faster than the Trump administration expected.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical supply disruption (Iran, refining capacity) is an under-appreciated near-term inflation input to watch alongside fiscal deficits, relevant for energy and inflation-hedge positioning.
insights.quote: you now have the Iran uh situation which is really uh putting upward pressure on oil

insights.claim: Magnificent 7 and other AI/data-center-driven stocks are trading at high valuations, and if interest rates and inflation keep rising there will be pricing pressure on these businesses regardless of whether they hit growth expectations.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Even if AI's growth narrative proves correct, current valuations leave little margin of safety against a higher-rate backdrop — a reason to trim concentrated AI/index exposure rather than assume the trade keeps working.
insights.quote: we all know the Magnificent 7 and all of the AI stocks, the data center sort of driven stocks, but these companies are trading at high valuations, no question about it.

insights.claim: The trillions of dollars being invested in AI will likely produce genuine technological gains but also overspending and overinvestment, with real uncertainty about token/algorithm pricing, margins and return on invested capital — a pattern typical of any investment boom that ends in write-offs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Expect eventual impairments/write-offs among AI infrastructure spenders; investors should stress-test AI capex assumptions on margins and ROIC rather than take current spending trajectories at face value.
insights.quote: There's trillions of dollars being spent and I think it's it's great in the sense that, you know, we're going to have a real revolution in AI, but it's very difficult to know the valuations and how much money is going to be made

insights.claim: After decades of roughly flat US/Canada electricity demand (offset by efficiency gains), AI data centers, robotics and EV growth are now pushing power demand growth to about 3-3.5% annually off a very large base, requiring a rebuild of grid infrastructure largely built in the 1960s-80s.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Structural electricity-demand growth from AI/EVs supports multi-year investment cases in power generation, transmission/grid buildout, and uranium/nuclear rather than just chip and hyperscaler names.
insights.quote: digitization is now starting to grow our energy by three 3% 3 and a half% which is really a large number off of a very large base.

insights.claim: Rather than owning AI/tech equities directly (some of which he views as grossly overvalued), the firm prefers owning the copper, silver and uranium that these technologies structurally require, given supply deficits, on a 3-5 year holding horizon.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: A 'picks and shovels' approach — owning structurally supply-constrained commodities feeding the AI/data-center/EV buildout — is framed as a lower-multiple, higher-conviction way to play the same growth theme.
insights.quote: some of them are grossly overvalued um in our view but they they won't survive and they won't be able to grow unless they have the metals and minerals

themes.theme: Gold, Currency Trust & Fixed Income Strategy

insights.claim: Given unfundable debt levels and the likelihood of financial repression and continued currency debasement, gold functions as a monetary substitute, and rising central-bank gold repatriation (e.g., the Netherlands, Germany) signals eroding trust between nations.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Central bank gold repatriation and financial-repression risk support maintaining or building strategic gold allocations as a currency/trust hedge, not just an inflation hedge.
insights.quote: I want to own a monetary substitute

insights.claim: Long-duration bonds have been one of the worst trades in recorded history over the past decade — TLT has round-tripped back to roughly 2004 levels, meaning a 2004 buyer would show no return after 22 years — but the advisor argues bonds are not permanently 'uninvestable'; his firm stays short-duration and plans to extend duration once rates peak and the economy slows.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the popular '60/40 is dead' narrative: watch for a peak in long rates as the signal to start extending bond duration for capital-gain potential rather than avoiding bonds indefinitely.
insights.quote: The TLT has been just eviscerated.

insights.claim: With the 10-year US Treasury yield near 5%, the 30-year around 5%+ and short rates near 4%, the currently high rate structure is pressuring the housing market, private credit and indebted households/businesses, which the advisor expects will eventually slow the economy enough to bring rates back down.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Elevated long-term yields are already stressing housing and private credit; a growth slowdown that forces rates lower is the trigger the advisor is watching before adding bond duration.
insights.quote: you're getting 5% close to 5% on the 10-year United States, you know, five 5.3 5.4% 4% on the 30-year and so forth.

insights.claim: Demographic decline is an under-discussed structural drag on debt sustainability: Japan has roughly a two-to-one ratio of deaths to births and is 'collapsing socially,' China's trend is nearly as bad, Russia's is also weak, the US is only slightly positive, and India remains a favorable outlier — shrinking populations undermine long-term economic capacity to service rising debt.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Countries with the worst demographic trends (Japan, China) face compounding debt-serviceability and growth headwinds, a factor to weigh alongside fiscal metrics when assessing sovereign risk and currency exposure.
insights.quote: you get a country like Japan and it has two to one the ratio of deaths to births. This is a country that's collapsing socially and if you if you collapse socially you can't thrive economically long term.

insights.claim: Rising nationalism and mistrust between nations — illustrated by an active US-Canada trade war despite the countries being close historical allies — alongside yen-carry-trade unwind risk and waning foreign appetite for Treasuries, reinforce the case for owning scarce, repriceable hard assets (infrastructure, gold, silver, copper, agriculture, energy).
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical fragmentation and de-dollarization pressures (carry-trade unwinds, reduced Treasury demand) add a currency/trust dimension to the case for hard-asset allocation beyond pure inflation hedging.
insights.quote: sign of the times, Canada and the US are in a trade war.

themes.theme: Case Study: Prairie Creek Silver Mine

insights.claim: The advisor personally visited Prairie Creek, a fully-developed silver-zinc-tungsten (and newly-valuable germanium) mine in Canada's Northwest Territories that the Hunt brothers built during their early-1980s silver-cornering run (when silver hit roughly $50/oz) and abandoned when prices crashed; some of the high-quality equipment left on site 50 years ago has as little as 1.6 hours of use, and it is now being restarted by Honey Badger Silver under CEO Chad Williams, with a proposed access road estimated at about $300 million against equipment already worth $300 million-plus on site.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Illustrates a real, identifiable silver/zinc/germanium restart optionality play tied to the structural commodity-deficit thesis, though the advisor flags meaningful execution and infrastructure risk (the Hunts themselves walked away).
insights.quote: one of the equipment had 1.6 hours on it.

insights.claim: Well-known resource investors are already shareholders in Honey Badger Silver, and the advisor's own firm has taken a small initial position while continuing to monitor the project's progress under CEO Chad Williams.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Wellum (CEO/CIO, Rocklinc)
insights.so_what: Co-investment by recognized resource-sector investors is a soft signal of quality for speculative silver-restart names, though position sizing here is small/exploratory rather than high-conviction.
insights.quote: Eric Sprat's an investor in it. Rick Rule's an investor in it.
